body: Hm, this might actually help paper over some of the pain points while we work on that git CLI release. I'll see if I have time to bench it later today.

Bad news: ran this on the rust repository using a new system I have, and the performance difference is not very large either way. Getting the status of the rust repository takes 115-125ms in all cases, whether using strict hash verification or not, whether or not there have been changes in the repo (for the sake of testing, I added a new file, deleted an existing file, modified some files, and stashed some changes).

It did seem to be about 5ms faster on average when strict verification is disabled, but over several trials, it seemed to swing a lot, and ultimately 5ms/125ms is not that much.

Now, this is one relatively speedy system running Linux, with a relatively small changeset, so there are other benchmarks I'd like to get before writing this off entirely:

- Lower powered systems
- Systems running MacOS/Windows
- git repos with very large changesets (or which are relatively dirty)

The good news is that it's pretty easy to test this change out: all you have to do is add `git2::opts::strict_hash_verification(false);` at the top of `main()`.

Additional testing performed on a copy of the rust repository on an NFS-ed system. Since the NFS cache seems to invalidate itself randomly and I don't have root, these were done with `--warmup 2` and any runs which had outliers (indicating the NFS cache might have been invalidated) were discarded.

On a clean copy of the rust repository:

- Current:
  Time (mean ± σ):      1.174 s ±  0.063 s    [User: 213.4 ms, System: 339.7 ms]
  Range (min … max):    1.089 s …  1.250 s    10 runs
- No strict:
  Time (mean ± σ):      1.238 s ±  0.163 s    [User: 184.9 ms, System: 368.6 ms]
  Range (min … max):    0.946 s …  1.604 s    10 runs

When the repository is slightly dirtied (one new file, one deleted file, one modified file, and one stash):

- Current:
     Time (mean ± σ):      1.157 s ±  0.182 s    [User: 189.1 ms, System: 357.8 ms]
     Range (min … max):    0.818 s …  1.313 s    10 runs
- No strict:
    Time (mean ± σ):      1.225 s ±  0.030 s    [User: 210.3 ms, System: 369.2 ms]
    Range (min … max):    1.151 s …  1.252 s    10 runs

Additional benchmarks on a CPU-bound Linux system (a VPS running with 1 virtual CPU and access to SSD-backed storage) shows similar trends.

There's a possibility that I'm actually just measuring the (shared) NFS remote's speed here, in which case these numbers are all nonsense. But it seems that hash verification is not our bottleneck, at least when simply requesting status.

If someone can demonstrate a use case in which this change makes a difference, I'll be happy to consider merging it, but I'm afraid this won't really result in improved perf.
